claims.text: Resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation in high-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings is primarily governed by in-situ interfacial barrier layers.
Thin oxide or compound films form at interfaces between deposited high-entropy-alloy layers.
Interfacial oxide or compound films inhibit dislocation motion and diffusion-mediated creep.
High-temperature thermal aging or cyclic thermal loading in an oxidizing atmosphere promotes controlled formation of interfacial oxide or compound layers.
Temperatures of 800–900 °C under sustained mechanical load can drive creep deformation in the proposed multilayer coating.
The relevant structural mediator is a continuous or semi-coherent oxide or compound layer between individual high-entropy-alloy layers.
Formation of the interfacial layers increases local residual compressive stress.
Interfacial layers create structural discontinuities that impede dislocation glide.
Interfacial layers impede atomic diffusion needed for time-dependent plastic deformation.
Restricting defect motion and atomic diffusion reduces the creep rate.
Oxidized, thermally aged multilayer coatings will show significantly lower creep strain than coatings processed to suppress interfacial oxidation under the same duration and load.
A comparable high-entropy-alloy multilayer coating fabricated under inert conditions exhibits conventional creep behavior.
The barrier mechanism is expected to operate between approximately 800 °C and 900 °C when oxidation occurs without overall coating degradation.
The barrier mechanism is expected to apply when diffusion-assisted deformation is dominant.
The protective effect may be diminished in non-oxidative or lower-temperature environments.
The cited AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 alloy showed reduced wear depth at 800 °C and its highest wear resistance at 900 °C.

contradictions.description: The prediction calls for comparison under identical mechanical loads and implicitly comparable thermal histories, but the experimental design describes one set as thermally aged in an oxidizing environment and the control as merely fabricated under inert conditions. Unless the control receives matched inert thermal aging, oxidation is confounded with thermal history.

The rule treats failure to form measurable barrier layers as falsification, although that outcome would show failure of the intervention or manipulation rather than falsify the claim that successfully formed barriers reduce creep.
